newsitem.title: USA: Future NATO chief backs Latam anti-drug center.
newsitem.headline: Future NATO chief backs Latam anti-drug center.

text.p: Gen. Wesley Clark, the head of U.S. military forces in Latin America and likely the next head of NATO, said on Wednesday that informal talks with Panama about creating an international anti-narcotics centre there had made good progress and he backed the idea.
"We've looked at it, a pretty clear convergence of interests has emerged, we have had very good and frank, open, informal discussions with the Panamanians," Clark told Reuters in an interview.

"Consideration of whether to move forward to formal negotation is underway. I am hopeful that this process will result in the creation of a multilateral counterdrugs centre, I think it is good for the United States and very good and very important for the region."

The United States and Panama have been holding preliminary talks to turn Howard Air Force Base, located at the Pacific entrance to the Panama Canal, into an international anti-drug centre. Howard runs about 8,000 counter-drug flights a year in the region.

"I am hopeful that this will come to pass," Clark said. "Narcotrafficking represents a threat to the territorial integrity, to the sovereignty, to the welfare, to the ecology of Latin America and the Caribbean."
"It can only be dealt with in a multilateral context ... no single nation by itself can hope to be effective."
Panamanian President Ernesto Perez Balladares said on Tuesday the centre, which he originally proposed, could function without U.S. participation, but on a smaller scale.

"Without the United States, the centre would not be as ambitious as we have proposed," Perez told local RPC radio. "It could operate as a Latin American centre, an instructional centre, an intelligence centre, but obviously it wouldn't be the same size as we envision it with the United States because the U.S. owns the specialised equipment."
Clark has said the centre would require a U.S. military presence of at least 2,000 to be operational. Panama has not officially said whether it would accept that.
The planned centre would likely not deploy multinational military forces to fight drug-trafficking but rather support action by sovereign national forces.

Perez has said his government would not negotiate retaining a U.S. military presence in Panama in the next century. But he has said the United States could keep Howard at no cost for use as an anti-drug centre.

The United States is to turn over control of the Panama Canal and withdraw all troops and bases by Dec. 31, 1999, in accordance with bilateral canal treaties. The U.S. Southern Command will move its headquarters to Miami later this year.

Clark is expected to face little difficulty in receiving formal approval from the U.S. Senate and NATO allies to replace retiring Gen. George Joulwan this summer as Supreme Allied Commander of NATO forces in Europe (SACEUR) based in Mons, Belgium.
He declined to discuss his new post ahead of his confirmation, although he said he was brushing up his Russian.
"I studied Russian for two years in school and I travelled in Russia as a cadet, in 1964. I had a conversational fluency in Russian which I hope to regain," he said.
